title: Not Just the Lining
subtitle: A blocked nose that a spray cannot fix, from the first visit to the splints coming out
description: Taking a history that separates lining from structure, the Cottle maneuver, relating the endoscopic findings to the internal nasal valve, choosing the graft, how much septum to leave, protecting the inferior turbinate, and recognizing a septal hematoma on day two.

steps.title: Step 1/7: The History
steps.scenario:
A 50-year-old man comes to clinic with years of nasal obstruction. You take the history before you touch him.

The block is on the left, it is there every day, and it does not move from side to side. He used an intranasal corticosteroid correctly for four months on his family doctor's advice and noticed almost no change. He also gets a watery nose some mornings. No facial pressure, no loss of smell.
steps.question: Which feature of the history points to a fixed structural cause rather than swollen lining?

options.text: (A) The watery rhinorrhea in the mornings
(B) A constant block on one side that does not switch sides and did not change after four months of a correctly used steroid spray
(C) Symptoms lasting for years
(D) The absence of facial pressure

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Swollen lining behaves in a recognizable way. It follows the nasal cycle, so the block moves from side to side through the day. It fluctuates with the season, with lying down, with exercise. And it responds to a steroid spray. A block that sits on one side, every day, and ignores four months of correct treatment is behaving like something that does not move: a deviated septum, a narrow valve, or both. That is the history of a structural obstruction, and it tells you what to look for when you examine him.

Why the others fail:
(A) A watery nose in the morning is a mucosal symptom, and he may well have some rhinitis alongside. But rhinitis alternates and responds to treatment. It does not explain a fixed left-sided block.
(C) Duration alone does not distinguish. Allergic rhinitis also lasts for years.
(D) No facial pressure argues against sinusitis, which is useful, but it does not tell you whether the remaining obstruction is lining or structure.

Keypoint: a one-sided block that never moves and never responds to a spray is structural until proven otherwise.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Clinical consensus statement: septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Clement PA, Gordts F; Standardisation Committee on Objective Assessment of the Nasal Airway, IRS, and ERS. Consensus report on acoustic rhinometry and rhinomanometry. Rhinology. 2005;43(3):169-179.

steps.title: Step 2/7: The Cottle Test
steps.scenario:
Before the endoscope, you test the nasal valve with your hands. You ask him to breathe in through the nose and rate the left side. Then you place a finger on his left cheek, draw the skin outward toward the ear, and ask him to breathe in again.

He says: a little better, but still blocked.
steps.media: Load image: Cottle maneuver, the examiner's fingers drawing the cheek laterally. Cummings Otolaryngology, 7th ed, Fig. 34-6, reproduced with Elsevier permission (obtain RightsLink license before deployment). Caption: 'Cottle maneuver. Reprinted from Kridel RWH et al. Cummings Otolaryngology, 7th ed. Elsevier; 2021, with permission.'
steps.question: Is this Cottle test positive or negative, and what does that tell you about where the block is?

options.text: (A) Weakly positive: pulling the cheek opened the valve a little, so the valve contributes, but most of the block is somewhere the maneuver cannot reach, such as the septum
(B) Negative: he is still blocked, so the valve plays no part and the septum is straight
(C) Positive: any improvement at all proves the valve is the whole problem and no septal work is needed
(D) The test is uninterpretable because it must be done with a probe inside the nose

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

What the test does. Drawing the cheek laterally pulls the lateral nasal wall outward, which widens the angle between the upper lateral cartilage and the septum, the internal nasal valve. So the test asks one question: if I open the valve from the outside, does he breathe better?

How to read it. A positive test means breathing improves clearly while you hold the cheek: the valve is at least part of the problem, and surgery that widens the valve should help. A negative test means nothing changes: the block is somewhere the maneuver cannot reach, most often the septum or the turbinate, and valve surgery alone will not fix it. In between, a small improvement means the valve contributes but is not the whole story.

His result. A little better, still blocked: weakly positive. Opening the valve helped, so the valve is narrow. But most of the obstruction stayed, so something else is holding the airway shut on the left, and from his history that is likely to be the septum. The test has told you to expect both a valve problem and a septal problem when you look with the scope, which is exactly what Step 3 will show.

The Cottle test has limits. It is subjective, and it can be falsely positive in a normal nose because pulling the cheek opens any valve a little. The modified Cottle is more specific: a cotton-tipped probe supports the upper lateral cartilage from inside, or the ala, so you can test one part of the lateral wall at a time. A patient who improves with the probe under the upper lateral cartilage has an internal valve problem; one who improves with the probe under the ala has an external valve problem.

Why the others fail:
(B) He did improve, so the test is not negative. And even a truly negative Cottle does not prove the septum is straight; it only says the lateral wall is not the cause.
(C) A small improvement is not proof that the valve is the whole problem. If it were, he would have said he could breathe freely with the cheek held. He did not.
(D) That describes the modified Cottle, which is a refinement, not a requirement. The classic Cottle is done on the cheek and is interpretable as it stands.

Keypoint: pull the cheek; clearly better means valve, no change means look elsewhere, a little better means both, and that is what he has.

Reference: Cottle MH. Rhino-sphygmo-manometry: an aid in physical diagnosis. Int Rhinol. 1968;6:7-26. Rhee JS, Poetker DM, Smith TL, et al. Nasal valve surgery improves disease-specific quality of life. Laryngoscope. 2005;115(3):437-440. Kridel RWH, Kelly PE, Holzapfel AM. The nasal septum. In: Flint PW, Francis HW, Haughey BH, et al, eds. Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery. 7th ed. Philadelphia, PA: Elsevier; 2021:484, Fig. 34-6. Reprinted with permission from Elsevier. Confirm edition and chapter number against the title page.

steps.title: Step 3/7: The Endoscopy
steps.scenario:
You pass a rigid endoscope. The caudal septum is deviated to the left and sits off the anterior nasal spine in the left vestibule. Higher up, the dorsal septum also curves left. On the left the angle between the septum and the upper lateral cartilage is visibly narrowed. Both inferior turbinates are moderately enlarged.

His complaint is a fixed left-sided block, and the Cottle test was weakly positive on that side.
steps.media: Load image: Anatomical illustration of the internal nasal valve, Daniel and Pálházi, Rhinoplasty: An Anatomical and Clinical Atlas, Fig. 4.31, reproduced with Springer Nature permission (obtain RightsLink license before deployment). Caption: 'Internal nasal valve. Reprinted from Daniel RK, Pálházi P. Rhinoplasty: An Anatomical and Clinical Atlas. Springer; 2018, with permission.'
steps.question: Where is the narrowest point of his airway, and which of the endoscopic findings is closing it?

options.text: (A) The nasopharynx; the enlarged turbinates are pushing air back
(B) The external nasal valve at the nostril; the deviated caudal septum is blocking the opening
(C) The olfactory cleft; the high dorsal deviation is closing it
(D) The internal nasal valve; the deviated septum is narrowing the angle with the upper lateral cartilage from the medial side

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The narrowest point of the nasal airway is the internal nasal valve, and it is where most of the resistance to breathing lives. Its walls are the septum medially, the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage superolaterally, the nasal floor below, and the head of the inferior turbinate behind. The angle between the septum and the upper lateral cartilage is normally 10 to 15 degrees. Because airflow resistance rises steeply as a passage narrows, a small loss of that angle produces a large increase in the effort of breathing.

Now put his findings on that anatomy. His septum deviates left, both at the caudal end and higher on the dorsum. On the left side the septum is therefore pushing into the valve from the medial wall, closing the angle with the upper lateral cartilage. That is the narrowing you saw, and it is the reason he feels blocked far more than the deviation looks. The Cottle maneuver pulled the lateral wall outward and opened the angle a little, which is why it helped a little. The turbinates are enlarged and will be dealt with, but they sit behind the valve and are not what is closing it.

Why the others fail:
(A) The nasopharynx is the widest part of the airway, not the narrowest, and turbinates do not push air backward.
(B) The external valve is the nostril opening, framed by the ala and the columella. His caudal septum does narrow the vestibule, but the fixed block he describes and the narrowing you saw are at the internal valve, one step further in.
(C) The olfactory cleft is high and narrow, but it is not a breathing passage. A high dorsal deviation affects the valve below it, not smell, and he has no smell complaint.

Keypoint: the internal valve is the narrowest point; a deviated septum closes it from the medial side, and that is where his block is.

Reference: Kasperbauer JL, Kern EB. Nasal valve physiology: implications in nasal surgery. Otolaryngol Clin North Am. 1987;20(4):699-719. Rhee JS, Poetker DM, Smith TL, et al. Nasal valve surgery improves disease-specific quality of life. Laryngoscope. 2005;115(3):437-440. Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Daniel RK, Pálházi P. Septum, turbinates, valves. In: Rhinoplasty: An Anatomical and Clinical Atlas. Cham, Switzerland: Springer; 2018:193, Fig. 4.31. Reprinted with permission from Springer Nature.

steps.title: Step 4/7: Which Graft
steps.scenario: The caudal and high dorsal deviations are severe enough that a standard submucous resection will not straighten the dorsum or open the valves. You plan an open functional rhinoplasty and turbinate reduction.
steps.media: Load image: Intraoperative photograph, open approach, unannotated: bilateral spreader grafts sutured between the dorsal septum and the upper lateral cartilages. Caption: 'Spreader grafts.'
steps.question: Which graft straightens a high dorsal deviation and widens the internal valve angle at the same time?

options.text: (A) Columellar strut graft
(B) Alar batten graft
(C) Spreader grafts
(D) Caudal septal extension graft

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Spreader grafts are strips of septal cartilage placed in a pocket between the dorsal septum and the upper lateral cartilage, then sutured through all three. They do two jobs. They splint the dorsal septum straight, and by holding the upper lateral cartilage away from the septum they widen the valve angle. They rebuild the T-shaped junction of the middle vault that a deviation has collapsed. They are the standard answer to a high dorsal deviation with valve narrowing.

A step further, for the surgeon rather than the student. Bilateral symmetric spreaders assume the septum is roughly central. When the septum itself is off center, as his caudal septum is, symmetric grafts widen the vault around the wrong midline. The alternative is to set a new midline with a caudal septal extension graft and splint the dorsal septum to it with a single extended spreader graft on the concave side. In the original series that corrected the dorsal deviation angle by 3.7 degrees and reduced nostril axis inclination by 11.7 degrees. It is the technique for a deviated cartilaginous vault when the midline has moved.

Why the others fail:
(A) A columellar strut supports the tip. It does not touch the dorsum or the internal valve.
(B) Alar battens reinforce the external valve, the ala and lateral crus, against collapse on inspiration. His problem is the internal valve.
(D) A caudal septal extension graft lengthens and supports the caudal septum and sets tip position. On its own it does nothing for the dorsum or the valve angle, though combined with a unilateral spreader it becomes the advanced answer above.

Keypoint: spreader grafts straighten the dorsal septum and open the internal valve; if the midline itself is displaced, build a new one first.

Reference: Rhee JS, Poetker DM, Smith TL, et al. Laryngoscope. 2005;115(3):437-440. Chen YY, Kim SA, Jang YJ. Centering a deviated nose by caudal septal extension graft and unilaterally extended spreader grafts. Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol. 2020;129(5):448-455. doi:10.1177/0003489419894617. Sheen JH. Spreader graft: a method of reconstructing the roof of the middle nasal vault following rhinoplasty. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1984;73(2):230-239.

steps.title: Step 5/7: How Much Septum to Leave
steps.scenario: You are inside the septum. You will harvest cartilage for the spreader grafts, and you need to know how much you can take.
steps.media: Load image: Your own line drawing of the quadrangular cartilage in profile, unannotated: dorsal edge, caudal edge, keystone junction with the nasal bones, and the anterior nasal spine. Caption: 'Septum in profile.'
steps.question: How much septum must you leave behind?

options.text: (A) None; the mucoperichondrial flaps hold the nose up
(B) An L-shaped strut of at least 10 mm along both the dorsal and the caudal edge, kept attached at the keystone and at the spine
(C) An L-shaped strut of 5 to 8 mm along each edge; that is enough in a small nose
(D) The caudal strut only, since that is what holds the tip

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The septum holds the nose up in two directions. The dorsal strut supports the middle vault: lose it and the dorsum drops into a saddle. The caudal strut supports the tip: lose it and the tip falls, the columella retracts, and the nose looks shorter. The L-strut is the part of the quadrangular cartilage that keeps both jobs, and the two places it must stay attached are the keystone, where cartilage meets nasal bone, and the anterior nasal spine. The usual minimum is 10 mm along each limb; in thin Asian cartilage 15 mm is safer. Everything posterior and inferior to that L can be harvested.

When the septum is not enough, which is common in Asian noses, you do not take more of the L-strut. You go elsewhere: conchal cartilage, or a bony batten from the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid.

Why the others fail:
(A) The flaps are lining, not structure. A nose without an L-strut collapses.
(C) This is the trap. An L of 5 to 8 mm looks like a strut and is not one. Below 10 mm the cartilage flexes under the load of the dorsum and the tip, and over months it warps or fractures. Ten millimeters is the minimum on each limb whatever the size of the nose, and in thin Asian cartilage 15 mm is safer.
(D) The caudal strut alone leaves nothing under the middle vault. Both limbs are needed, and the corner between them at the keystone is the most important part.

Keypoint: leave an L, at least 10 to 15 mm on each limb, attached at the keystone and the spine; when you need more cartilage, take it from somewhere else.

Reference: Gubisch W. Twenty-five years experience with extracorporeal septoplasty. Facial Plast Surg. 2006;22(4):230-239. Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Clinical consensus statement: septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435.

steps.title: Step 6/7: The Turbinate
steps.scenario:
His inferior turbinates are enlarged and are part of the picture. You will reduce them in the same operation as the septum and the valve.

You choose a submucosal technique rather than removing the turbinate.
steps.media: Load image: Endoscopic view of submucosal inferior turbinate reduction, mucosa preserved, unannotated. Caption: 'Submucosal reduction.'
steps.question: Which complication are you avoiding by preserving the mucosa?

options.text: (A) Cerebrospinal fluid leak
(B) Toxic shock syndrome
(C) Anosmia
(D) Empty nose syndrome

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The inferior turbinate is not just a lump in the airway. Its mucosa warms and humidifies air and, more importantly, senses it: the feeling of breathing through the nose comes from receptors in that lining. Remove too much and you get a paradox. The airway is wide open on the scope, and the patient says he cannot breathe. That is empty nose syndrome, and there is no good treatment for it. So the turbinate is reduced from underneath, taking bone and submucosal tissue and leaving the surface intact. The consensus statement says the same: when the turbinate is reduced, the mucosa should be preserved.

Why the others fail:
(A) A CSF leak comes from the skull base, well above the inferior turbinate. It is not a turbinate surgery complication.
(B) Toxic shock is a complication of prolonged nasal packing, not of how much turbinate is removed. It is one of the reasons packing is avoided in Step 6.
(C) Smell lives on the olfactory cleft, high in the nose. The inferior turbinate does not carry it.

Keypoint: reduce the turbinate from underneath and keep the lining; a wide nose that cannot feel air is worse than the block you started with.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Coste A, Dessi P, Serrano E. Empty nose syndrome. Eur Ann Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Dis. 2012;129(2):93-97.

steps.title: Step 7/7: Day Two
steps.scenario:
Septum straightened and grafted, valves open, turbinates reduced. You placed septal splints and sent him home the same day, breathing through his nose.

On the second postoperative day he calls. Both sides have blocked up completely since last night, the pain across the bridge is worse than yesterday, and he feels feverish.
steps.media: Load image: Endoscopic view of a septal hematoma, unannotated: smooth, bulging, bluish swelling of the septum on both sides. Caption: 'Day two.'
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: (A) See him today and look at the septum. A bilateral fluctuant swelling is a hematoma: incise and drain it, close the dead space with quilting sutures or splints, cover with an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic, and see him again within one to two days
(B) Reassure him; swelling and blockage are expected for the first week
(C) Aspirate it with a needle in clinic and send him home
(D) Start oral antibiotics by phone and review at the planned one-week visit

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

A nose that was open on the day of surgery and has closed on both sides by day two is a septal hematoma until you have looked and proved otherwise. Blood collects between the cartilage and the mucoperichondrial flap. The cartilage has no blood supply of its own; it lives off that flap, and once the flap is lifted away the cartilage starts to die. Left alone, the collection becomes an abscess within days, and the end result is a saddle nose. The examination takes a minute: a smooth, bulging, often bluish swelling of the septum, soft to a probe, usually on both sides because blood tracks across the dissection plane.

Management is the same everywhere. In a systematic review of 503 patients, every case was treated by incision and drainage. A short inferior mucosal incision on one or both sides, evacuate the clot, then close the dead space so it cannot refill: through-and-through quilting sutures or splints pressed against both flaps, either one, the point is to hold the flap back down on the cartilage. Cover with an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic while the splints are in, because the space is now at risk of infection, and if there was pus or he was febrile, treat it as an abscess: culture, a small drain, and antibiotics until it stops. Then see him again in one to two days to make sure it has not reaccumulated; in the review the re-collection rate was 3.6 percent.

Why the others fail:
(B) Some congestion in week one is normal. Complete bilateral obstruction that appeared overnight, with pain getting worse instead of better, is not.
(C) Needle aspiration on its own is often not enough; clot re-forms and the space refills. A formal incision that lets it drain, followed by closure of the dead space, is what holds.
(D) Antibiotics do not drain a hematoma. By the one-week visit the cartilage may already be lost.

Keypoint: bilateral obstruction after septoplasty that gets worse instead of better is a hematoma until proven otherwise; drain it today, close the space, and look again in two days.

Reference: Jackson R, Jia W, Edafe O. Evaluation of the management of nasal septal haematoma and abscess: a systematic review. J Laryngol Otol. 2025. PMID: 39434415. Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Clinical consensus statement: septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Cheng LH, Wu PC, Shih CP, et al. Nasal septal abscess: a 10-year retrospective study. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2019. doi:10.1007/s00405-018-5212-0.
